slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 1/8
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; cerebrospinal fluid if nervous system involvement is suspected

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 2/8
bullets: What it is used for: Testing is done with symptoms of syphilis or if a sex partner was recently diagnosed. Second-stage symptoms include fever and swollen glands, a rough red rash usually on the palms or soles, headache or muscle aches, sore throat, fatigue, weight loss and patchy hair loss.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 3/8
bullets: With high risk (multiple partners, sex without a condom, HIV, another sexually transmitted disease, sex with men who have sex with men), regular testing is advised even without symptoms.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 4/8
bullets: Syphilis testing is needed in pregnancy: passing the infection to the fetus can cause serious, sometimes deadly problems. CDC recommends testing at the first prenatal visit and, with higher risk, again at 28 weeks and at delivery.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 5/8
bullets: Physiology: Syphilis tests usually look for antibodies to the bacterium that causes syphilis. The first step is screening: RPR (an antibody called reagin) or VDRL (on blood or spinal fluid, a broader range of antibodies). These antibodies are also made in some autoimmune diseases and other infections, so a positive screen is followed by a second, confirmatory test.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 6/8
bullets: The confirmatory test usually looks for antibodies the immune system makes only against syphilis (e.g., TP-PA, TPHA, FTA-ABS, enzyme or chemiluminescence immunoassays). If present, the person either has syphilis now or had syphilis that was treated. Sometimes the bacteria themselves are looked for instead, but only specialized labs can do this.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 7/8
bullets: Syphilis spreads through vaginal, oral or anal sex and can pass to a fetus during pregnancy. The first stage starts 2–12 weeks after exposure with a painless sore (chancre) that can go unnoticed; the second starts 1–6 months after the chancre heals; untreated, a latent stage lasting years follows — without symptoms the infection can still spread and cause damage; the fourth stage brings severe problems such as dementia and blindness.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 8/8
bullets: It is easiest to cure early.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Positive result: Per CDC, a presumptive diagnosis of syphilis requires two kinds of serologic tests: a nontreponemal test (VDRL or RPR) and a treponemal test (TP-PA, various enzyme and chemiluminescence immunoassays, immunoblots or rapid treponemal assays). One type alone is insufficient. Anyone with a reactive nontreponemal test should get a treponemal test to confirm the diagnosis (traditional algorithm).

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Positive result: Some labs use a reverse sequence: an automated treponemal immunoassay (EIA or CIA) first and, if positive, a quantitative nontreponemal test with titer. If the nontreponemal test is negative, a different treponemal test (preferably TP-PA) adjudicates. If that second treponemal test is also negative and the risk is low, no further evaluation or treatment is indicated.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Positive result: If the follow-up test confirms syphilis, treatment is usually penicillin: antibiotics cure most early-stage infections, but in later stages cannot undo damage already done. Sex partners should be told so they can be tested and treated if needed, and screening tests are repeated to check how well treatment is working.

Negative result: A negative screening result means you probably do not have syphilis, but it does not completely rule it out: antibodies can take a couple of weeks to develop. Another test may be needed after a suspected exposure.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a blood test. If syphilis may be affecting the brain, spinal cord or nerves, cerebrospinal fluid is tested via a lumbar puncture, before which you may be asked to empty your bladder and bowels. At-home blood collection kits are screening tests only — another test is needed to confirm the diagnosis.

Interferences: False-positive nontreponemal results can occur with conditions unrelated to syphilis: other infections (e.g., HIV), autoimmune conditions, vaccinations, injection drug use, pregnancy and older age.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Limitations: Nontreponemal titers can reflect disease activity and are used to monitor treatment; results are reported quantitatively (highest titer). A fourfold change (two dilutions, e.g., from 1:16 to 1:4) is needed for a clinically significant difference. Serial tests use the same method (VDRL or RPR), preferably in the same lab: VDRL and RPR titers cannot be compared directly, and RPR titers are often slightly higher.

Most patients with a reactive treponemal test stay reactive for life, regardless of treatment or disease activity (15%–25% of those treated in the primary stage become nonreactive after 2–3 years). Treponemal antibody titers do not predict treatment response and should not be used for that purpose.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: No single test diagnoses neurosyphilis: CSF findings (cell count, protein, CSF-VDRL), blood serology and neurologic signs are assessed together. CSF-VDRL is highly specific but insensitive; CSF FTA-ABS is less specific but highly sensitive.

In certain parts of the world, bacteria closely related to the syphilis bacterium spread through non-sexual skin contact with sores and cause yaws, bejel and pinta. Blood tests cannot tell them apart from syphilis — the provider relies on the skin sores and medical and travel history.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Vaginal discharge (swab; slides with saline and 10% KOH)

What it is used for: Done to find the cause of vaginal discharge, itching, burning or odour. The infections most often responsible are bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and vulvovaginal candidiasis; cervicitis can also cause discharge. CDC notes that history alone is not enough for an accurate diagnosis, so examination and laboratory testing are needed.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: Method: vaginal pH is measured with pH paper (pH > 4.5 is common with BV or trichomoniasis, though trichomoniasis can occur at normal pH). One sample is diluted in 1–2 drops of 0.9% saline and a second in 10% KOH; an amine (fishy) odour right after adding KOH suggests BV or trichomoniasis.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: With coverslips in place, slides are examined at low and high power: the saline slide may show motile trichomonads or clue cells (epithelial cells whose borders are obscured by small bacteria); the KOH slide shows hyphae or blastospores of candidiasis.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 1/3
cols: BV is diagnosed by the Amsel criteria — at least three of four: homogeneous thin (milk-like) discharge smoothly coating the vaginal walls; clue cells on microscopy; vaginal fluid pH > 4.5; a fishy odour before or after adding 10% KOH (whiff test).

Absence of trichomonads in saline or fungal elements in KOH does not rule out these infections: microscopy is about 50% sensitive compared with NAAT (trichomoniasis) or culture (yeast). For trichomoniasis the wet mount is 44–68% sensitive, so a negative wet mount should be followed by a molecular test when possible.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 2/3
cols: The laboratory reference standard is the Nugent score on a Gram-stained smear: 0–3 Lactobacillus-predominant, 4–6 intermediate, 7–10 BV.
Motile trichomonads mean trichomoniasis; the provider prescribes treatment, partners should be tested, and testing for other STIs is advised.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 3/3
cols: Many white cells without trichomonads or yeast may indicate cervicitis.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample is taken from vaginal discharge with a cotton swab or stick during a speculum exam. Usually tampons, vaginal creams or medicines and vaginal sex are avoided for 24 hours before. Read the slide immediately: wet-mount sensitivity for trichomonads drops to 20% within one hour of collection.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Per the official source, avoid tampons, vaginal creams and medicines, and vaginal sex for 24 hours before sampling. The textbook is stricter: no swab during a period or for 1–2 days after it, and vaginal suppositories and tablets stopped 2–3 days before — follow your laboratory’s instructions.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Limitations: A pH test alone cannot diagnose BV (healthy vaginal pH is 3.8–4.5). Pap tests are of no use for BV, and culture of Gardnerella vaginalis is not recommended because it is not specific. BV NAATs are for symptomatic women only.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Cervical cells (clinician-collected) or a self-collected vaginal swab

What it is used for: The HPV test looks in a sample of cervical cells for the infection that causes precancer and cancer. It is done alone (primary screening), with a Pap test (cotesting), or after an abnormal Pap — for example, ASC-US, to see whether HPV caused the changes. The screening schedule is on the Pap test card.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses: low-risk types cause warts, while high-risk types can cause cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar, vaginal and penile cancers. The test detects DNA or RNA from high-risk HPV. HPV usually spreads through sexual contact, is especially common at ages 21–29, and usually clears on its own within a year or two.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: A positive result means high-risk HPV was found. It does not mean you have or will get precancer or cancer, but it raises future risk. There is no treatment for the HPV infection itself; next steps (colposcopy, more frequent testing) depend on past results, age and other factors.
A negative result means high-risk HPV was not found. Per NCI, the next test is in 5 years; you may need to return sooner if you had abnormal results in the past.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: A positive test after several negative ones is not necessarily a new infection: HPV can become active again after many years. Whether a reactivated infection carries the same risk as a new one is not known.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample is taken by the provider from the cervix with a speculum and soft brush, or self-collected in a clinic by inserting and rotating a swab in the vagina. An HPV test alone needs no preparation. For 2 days before a cotest, avoid vaginal sex, douching, vaginal medicines and spermicides; tell the provider about recent sex or a period.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: A Pap smear (cotest) is not done during a period — about 5 days after it ends is a good time; for 2 days before, avoid tampons, vaginal creams and medicines, douching and vaginal sex. An HPV test alone needs no preparation; tell the provider if you have your period. The textbook advises stopping vaginal suppositories 2–3 days before.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Limitations: HPV vaccination does not prevent infection with all high-risk types, so vaccinated people should still be screened.

Self-collected HPV testing may improve access to screening; in a pooled analysis of studies in China, however, self-collected samples were less sensitive for CIN 2+ (about 86%) than physician-collected samples (about 97%).

slides.title: Syphilis
bullets: A presumptive diagnosis requires two types of serologic tests: nontreponemal (VDRL, RPR) and treponemal (TP-PA, EIAs/CIAs, immunoblots, rapid tests). One type alone is insufficient: it can give false negatives in primary syphilis and false positives in people without syphilis or previously treated.

slides.title: Syphilis
rows: Nontreponemal test; a reactive result is confirmed with a treponemal test (traditional algorithm).
Treponemal test; in the reverse sequence algorithm it may be used as the first screen.

slides.title: Syphilis
rows: With signs of neurosyphilis (cranial nerve dysfunction, meningitis, stroke, altered mental status, loss of vibration sense) cerebrospinal fluid is examined.
Treatment response is monitored with nontreponemal titers; sequential tests should use the same method, ideally in the same laboratory.

slides.title: Syphilis
rows: Syphilis is likely — interpreted with the clinical stage and treatment history.
A different treponemal test resolves the result; treponemal tests usually stay reactive for life, even after treatment.
A false positive is possible: HIV, autoimmune disease, vaccination, injecting drug use, pregnancy, older age.

slides.title: Syphilis
bullets: VDRL and RPR titers cannot be compared directly.

slides.title: Lactobacilli (Döderlein bacilli)
slides.caption:
1 — Long rods staining purple on Gram.
2 — An epithelial cell for comparison.
What it looks like: Long thin rods, abundant in the background and on cells.
Key feature: Many long rods, few cocci.

slides.title: Lactobacilli (Döderlein bacilli)
slides.caption:
What it means: Normal vaginal flora; keeps the environment acidic. When abundant, intermediate cells may be lysed (cytolysis).
Stain / preparation: Gram; also visible on Pap
Caveat: Rod shape does not identify the species; there is no single "normal count".

slides.title: Clue cell
slides.caption:
1 — Small bacteria densely adhering to the cell surface.
2 — Bacteria blur the cell border as well.
What it looks like: A squamous cell covered with small coccobacilli; shaggy, indistinct borders. Few lactobacilli in the background.

slides.title: Clue cell
slides.caption:
Key feature: The cell border is obscured by bacteria.
What it means: A sign of bacterial vaginosis (one of Amsel’s criteria). The clinician diagnoses on the full set of criteria.
Confused with: An ordinary cell with a few bacteria — if the edges are still sharp, it is not a clue cell.

slides.title: Clue cell
slides.caption:
Stain / preparation: Wet mount / Gram / Pap
Caveat: One sign of bacterial vaginosis; never a diagnosis on its own.

slides.title: Trichomonas vaginalis
slides.caption:
1 — Pear-shaped body; nucleus in the broad anterior part.
2 — Four anterior flagella; recurrent flagellum, undulating membrane and axostyle.

slides.title: Trichomonas vaginalis
slides.caption:
What it looks like: Pear-shaped grey-green body with a pale, elongated, eccentric nucleus and red cytoplasmic granules. Flagella are often not seen in stained smears.
Key feature: Pear shape + pale eccentric nucleus. Motile in a wet mount.

slides.title: Trichomonas vaginalis
slides.caption:
What it means: Trichomoniasis, usually with many neutrophils. A sensitive test (NAAT) is recommended to confirm.
Confused with: Cell fragments, degenerated leukocytes.
Stain / preparation: Wet mount or stained smear

slides.title: Trichomonas vaginalis
slides.caption: Caveat: A structural diagram. Wet mounts show motility; flagella may not be visible on Pap. A negative wet mount does not exclude infection.

slides.title: Candida (yeast)
slides.caption:
1 — Budding oval yeast cells.
2 — Pseudohypha: joined elongated cells with constrictions at the junctions.
What it looks like: Budding oval yeasts and segmented pseudohyphae; hyphae "skewer" epithelial cells.
Key feature: Segmented threads + budding yeasts.

slides.title: Candida (yeast)
slides.caption:
What it means: Consistent with vulvovaginal candidiasis; asymptomatic colonisation is possible — judge with the clinical picture.
Stain / preparation: KOH / Gram / Pap
Caveat: Not every Candida species forms pseudohyphae; interpret with symptoms and tests.

slides.title: Inflammation (many neutrophils)
slides.caption:
1 — Neutrophils with multilobed nuclei.
2 — A large epithelial cell for comparison.
What it looks like: Many segmented neutrophils among and over epithelial cells.
Key feature: More leukocytes than epithelial cells.

slides.title: Inflammation (many neutrophils)
slides.caption:
What it means: A sign of inflammation (e.g. trichomoniasis, cervicitis). Heavy inflammation can obscure epithelium and limit assessment.
Stain / preparation: Pap or another stained smear
Caveat: Many neutrophils signal inflammation but not its cause.

slides.title: Gonococci (Gram stain)
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — Neutrophil with a multilobed nucleus.
2 — Pink-red, paired, bean-shaped cocci in the cytoplasm (drawn enlarged).
What it looks like: Paired, bean-shaped, red-pink (Gram-negative) diplococci with facing concave sides — inside neutrophils.

slides.title: Gonococci (Gram stain)
slides.caption:
Key feature: Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci.
What it means: Highly reliable for gonorrhoea in male urethral smears. Low sensitivity in cervical smears — NAAT is recommended.
Stain / preparation: Gram

slides.title: Gonococci (Gram stain)
slides.caption: Caveat: A negative endocervical Gram smear does not exclude gonorrhoea — NAAT may be needed.

slides.title: Koilocyte
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — A sharply bordered, irregular perinuclear cavity (halo).
2 — Enlarged dark nucleus with an irregular outline; dense cytoplasm at the rim.

slides.title: Koilocyte
slides.caption:
What it looks like: A large clear perinuclear cavity with a sharp edge (halo) and a dense cytoplasmic rim. Enlarged, dark, irregular ("raisinoid") nucleus, often binucleate.
Key feature: Halo + abnormal nucleus. A plain nucleus means it is not one.
What it means: A sign of HPV effect; reported as LSIL in Bethesda.

slides.title: Koilocyte
slides.caption:
Confused with: Small perinuclear clearing (glycogen, inflammation) — vague edge and a normal nucleus.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A halo alone is not enough: nuclear atypia must be present.

slides.title: HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, scant cytoplasm.
2 — Irregular nuclear outline, coarse dark chromatin.

slides.title: HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
slides.caption:
What it looks like: Small immature cells, often in groups. The nucleus fills most of the cell; dark, irregular, coarse chromatin.
Key feature: High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Compare with an intermediate nucleus.

slides.title: HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
slides.caption:
What it means: High likelihood of a precancerous lesion. The clinician decides next steps per ASCCP 2019 — colposcopy or expedited treatment. The cytologist reports.
Confused with: Parabasal and metaplastic cells — smooth nuclei, fine chromatin.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)

slides.title: HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
slides.caption: Caveat: The drawing explains HSIL features; a cytologist makes the final call.

slides.title: A screening RPR is reactive. Which next step fits the source?
options: Syphilis is confirmed — treatment and partner notification without other tests are enough
The result is false: RPR is reliable only in spinal fluid
A treponemal test (e.g., TP-PA or an immunoassay)
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. A reactive nontreponemal test should always be followed by a treponemal test.

Basis: Nontreponemal tests can be reactive in other conditions; diagnosis needs two kinds of tests.

slides.title: What is needed to diagnose BV by the Amsel criteria?
options: At least three of the four criteria
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: At least three of four: homogeneous thin discharge, clue cells, pH > 4.5, fishy odour with KOH.

slides.title: A vaginal wet mount was read 2 hours after collection; no trichomonads were seen. Conclusion?
options: A KOH mount shows trichomonads better
Unreliable; confirm with a molecular test (NAAT)
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The slide should have been read immediately.

Basis: CDC: sensitivity drops to 20% within an hour; NAAT is advised after a negative wet mount.

slides.title: Which bacterioscopic method is more effective in diagnosing gonorrhea in women:
options: bacterioscopy of smears stained with methylene blue
bacterioscopy of smears stained by Gram
examination of smears stained by Romanowsky

slides.title: When which infection is detected is testing for gonorrhea appropriate:
Etiology and pathogenesis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis?
bullets: 1. The causative agent of gonorrhea is Neisseria gonorrhoeae: gram-negative, bean-shaped diplococcus, located inside leukocytes; transmitted mainly sexually, at birth to the newborn (conjunctivitis).

2. Pathogenesis: attachment to columnar epithelium (urethra, cervical canal, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva) via pili and membrane proteins, invasion, purulent inflammation; often asymptomatic in women, complications – pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, dissemination.
3. The causative agent of trichomoniasis is Trichomonas vaginalis: a pear-shaped, flagellated, motile unicellular parasite; transmitted sexually.

slides.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis?
bullets: 4. Pathogenesis of trichomoniasis: attachment to the epithelium of the vagina and urethra and cytotoxic effect, inflammation (many leukocytes), rise in pH; often asymptomatic in men; pregnancy complications, increases the risk of HIV transmission.
5. Both infections may coexist with other STIs – comprehensive testing.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis?
bullets: 1. Gonorrhea: NAAT is the main method (vaginal swab in women, first-void urine in men; extragenital sites); in men with symptomatic urethritis, intracellular diplococci in leukocytes on a Gram or methylene blue smear – a presumptive diagnosis (low sensitivity in women).
2. Gonococcal culture on selective media – to determine antibiotic susceptibility (in treatment failure), confirmation by two methods.
3. Trichomoniasis: NAAT – highly sensitive; wet mount (sensitivity 44–68%, falls sharply after 1 hour – examine immediately), culture (InPouch) – for resistance; the PAP test is not diagnostic.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis?
bullets: 4. In stained smears (Romanowsky) the shape and nucleus of trichomonads are seen, but motility is not.
5. In both infections also test for chlamydia, syphilis, HIV; retest after treatment.

slides.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis, laboratory diagnosis?
bullets: 1. Gonorrhea: N. gonorrhoeae – a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus; infects columnar epithelium, purulent urethritis/cervicitis, often asymptomatic (women), complications – pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility.
2. Trichomoniasis: T. vaginalis – a flagellated motile protozoan; vaginitis, urethritis; often asymptomatic (men).
3. Diagnosis of gonorrhea: NAAT (main), in men a Gram/methylene blue smear (intracellular diplococci), culture and antibiotic susceptibility.

slides.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis, laboratory diagnosis?
bullets: 4. Diagnosis of trichomoniasis: NAAT (highly sensitive), wet mount (immediately; sensitivity 44–68%), culture; if found on a PAP test – confirm with a sensitive test.
5. Test together for other STIs (chlamydia, syphilis, HIV) and treat sexual partners.
